title: The Class Equation: Partitioning a Group by Conjugacy
content: The class equation |G| = |Z(G)| + Σ [G:C_G(x)] is one of the fundamental structural results in finite group theory. It arises from decomposing G into orbits under conjugation: G acts on itself by g·x = gxg⁻¹, with orbits = conjugacy classes and stabilizers = centralizers. The central elements form singleton orbits (fixed points), while non-central elements contribute orbits of size [G:C_G(x)] > 1. This file proves the class equation from Mathlib's `Group.nat_card_center_add_sum_card_noncenter_eq_card`, establishes the full orbit-centralizer formula, and derives the p-group corollaries.
mathContext: **Class equation**: $|G| = |Z(G)| + \sum_{x \in T} [G : C_G(x)]$ where $T$ is a set of representatives for non-central conjugacy classes. **Derivation**: G is partitioned into conjugacy classes $[x] = \{gxg^{-1} \mid g \in G\}$; each $[x]$ has size $[G:C_G(x)]$ (orbit-stabilizer); summing: $|G| = \sum_{[x]} |[x]| = |Z(G)| + \sum_{\text{non-central}} |[x]|$. **Historical hierarchy**: Lagrange → Orbit-Stabilizer → Burnside → Class Equation → p-Group Theory.

title: Class Equation from Mathlib: One-Line Application
content: `class_equation` proves |Z(G)| + Σ_{noncenter} |c| = |G| by direct application of Mathlib's `Group.nat_card_center_add_sum_card_noncenter_eq_card`. This theorem was added to Mathlib (Mathlib.GroupTheory.ClassEquation) precisely for this kind of formalization. The Lean proof is essentially a one-line application; the symmetric form `class_equation_symm` is just `.symm`. The mathematical work is in the orbit-stabilizer section that follows, which proves the quantitative identity |[x]| = [G:C_G(x)] that gives each non-central summand its concrete value.
mathContext: `Group.nat_card_center_add_sum_card_noncenter_eq_card [Group G] [Finite G]`: $\text{Nat.card}(\text{center}\,G) + \sum_{c \in \text{ConjClasses.noncenter}\,G} \text{Nat.card}(c.carrier) = \text{Nat.card}(G)$. Here $\sum^f$ is the finitely-supported sum which, for finite $G$, equals an ordinary $\Sigma$. Each $c \in $ `ConjClasses.noncenter` corresponds to a non-singleton conjugacy class.

title: Orbit = Conjugacy Class Carrier
content: `conj_orbit_eq_carrier` proves that the orbit of x under the ConjAct G action equals the carrier of the conjugacy class of x. Both sides describe {gxg⁻¹ : g ∈ G}. The proof unfolds `mem_orbit_iff`, `ConjClasses.mem_carrier_iff_isConj`, and `IsConj`/`SemiconjBy`, then provides forward/backward witnesses: from `c • x = y` extract `g = ConjAct.ofConjAct c`; from `g * x = y * g` (the SemiconjBy form) use `ConjAct.toConjAct g` as the orbit witness. Both directions close with `calc` blocks and the `group` tactic for group-arithmetic normalization.
mathContext: Goal: $\text{orbit}(\mathrm{ConjAct}\,G, x) = (\mathrm{ConjClasses.mk}\,x).\text{carrier}$. Forward: if $c \cdot x = y$ then with $g = \mathrm{ofConjAct}(c)$, $gxg^{-1} = y$, so $gx = ygg^{-1} \cdot g = yg$, witnessing `SemiconjBy`. Backward: if $gx = yg$ (i.e., $\mathrm{IsConj}\,x\,y$), then $\mathrm{toConjAct}(g) \cdot x = gxg^{-1} = ygg^{-1} = y$. The `group` tactic normalizes $gg^{-1}$ cancellations.

title: Stabilizer (pulled back) = Centralizer
content: `conj_stabilizer_eq_centralizer` identifies the conjugation stabilizer with C_G(x), but states it precisely: the stabilizer lives in `ConjAct G`, so the actual identity is `(stabilizer (ConjAct G) x).comap ConjAct.toConjAct = centralizer {x}`. After unfolding `Subgroup.mem_comap`, `mem_stabilizer_iff`, `ConjAct.toConjAct_smul`, and `mem_centralizer_iff`, the bidirectional reduction is between `g * x * g⁻¹ = x` and `g * x = x * g` — two routine algebraic manipulations using `group` and a single `rw`. This `comap` formulation is exactly what `Subgroup.index_comap_of_surjective` consumes in the next theorem.
mathContext: Goal: $(\text{stab}_{\mathrm{ConjAct}\,G}(x))^* = C_G(\{x\})$ where $(-)^*$ denotes `comap` under `ConjAct.toConjAct`. Pointwise: $g \in \text{stab}^* \iff gxg^{-1} = x \iff gx = xg \iff g \in C_G(x)$. Forward: $g \cdot x \stackrel{(\cdot g^{-1} \cdot g)}{=} gxg^{-1} \cdot g = xg$. Backward: $gxg^{-1} = xgg^{-1} = x$.

title: Orbit-Centralizer Identity via index_comap_of_surjective
content: `card_conjClass_eq_centralizer_index` closes |[x]| = [G:C_G(x)] in two clean steps that avoid the divisibility shuffles typical of orbit-stabilizer proofs over Nat. Step 1 uses `Subgroup.index_eq_card` plus `MulAction.orbitEquivQuotientStabilizer` to rewrite `Nat.card (orbit)` as `(stabilizer).index`. Step 2 uses `Subgroup.index_comap_of_surjective` applied to the surjective iso `ConjAct.toConjAct : G ≃* ConjAct G`: because the centralizer is the comap of the conjugation stabilizer (previous lemma), their indices agree. This is a reusable pattern: any orbit-cardinality lemma involving a group iso can be closed by recognizing the relevant subgroup as a comap and invoking `index_comap_of_surjective`.
mathContext: Goal: $|[x]| = [G : C_G(x)]$. **Step 1** (orbit-stabilizer over `ConjAct G`): $|\text{orbit}(\mathrm{ConjAct}\,G, x)| = [\mathrm{ConjAct}\,G : \text{stab}(x)]$ via `orbitEquivQuotientStabilizer` (which gives `orbit ≃ G/stab` as types). **Step 2** (transfer along iso): $[\mathrm{ConjAct}\,G : \text{stab}(x)] = [G : (\text{stab}(x))^*]$ via `index_comap_of_surjective` for surjective $\mathrm{toConjAct}$; and the comap is $C_G(x)$ by `conj_stabilizer_eq_centralizer`.

title: Singleton Class ↔ Central Element
content: `card_conjClass_eq_one_iff_mem_center` proves |[x]| = 1 ↔ x ∈ Z(G), the qualitative complement of the orbit-centralizer formula. Forward: if the orbit is a singleton, then for every g, `ConjAct.toConjAct g • x = x` (both are in the orbit, which is a singleton), unfolding to `gxg⁻¹ = x` then `gx = xg`. Backward: if x ∈ Z(G), then for any orbit element `c • x = ConjAct.ofConjAct c · x · (ConjAct.ofConjAct c)⁻¹`, commutativity gives `= x`. The proof uses `Nat.card_eq_one_iff_unique` to translate between cardinality-1 and unique-element formulations.
mathContext: Goal: $|[x]| = 1 \iff x \in Z(G)$. Forward: $|[x]| = 1 \Rightarrow$ for any orbit elements $a, b$, $a = b$. Take $a = (\mathrm{toConjAct}\,g) \cdot x$ and $b = x$: both lie in the orbit, so $gxg^{-1} = x$, hence $gx = xg$. Backward: $x \in Z(G) \Rightarrow $ for $c \in \mathrm{ConjAct}\,G$ with witness $c \cdot x = y$, $y = (\mathrm{ofConjAct}\,c) \cdot x \cdot (\mathrm{ofConjAct}\,c)^{-1} = x \cdot (\mathrm{ofConjAct}\,c) \cdot (\mathrm{ofConjAct}\,c)^{-1} = x$.

title: p-Group Applications: Center Nontriviality and p²-Abelian
content: Three p-group results follow directly from the class equation infrastructure. `pgroup_fixed_point` packages `IsPGroup.card_modEq_card_fixedPoints`: |X| ≡ |Fix(G,X)| (mod p) for any p-group action. `center_nontrivial_of_pgroup` extracts the most-used corollary: nontrivial p-groups have nontrivial center (mod-p argument on the class equation). `p_sq_group_comm` uses `IsPGroup.commGroupOfCardEqPrimeSq` to conclude groups of order p² are abelian — formalizing the classical pipeline Z(G) ⊆ G with |G/Z(G)| ∈ {1, p}, so G/Z(G) cyclic forces G abelian.
mathContext: **Center nontriviality**: $p \mid |G|$ and each non-central $[x]$ has $p \mid |[x]|$ (since $|[x]| \mid p^k$ and $|[x]| > 1$). Class equation mod $p$: $0 \equiv |Z(G)| \pmod p$, so $p \mid |Z(G)|$, hence $Z(G) \neq \{e\}$. **$p^2$-groups abelian**: $|G| = p^2$, $p \mid |Z(G)|$, so $|Z(G)| \in \{p, p^2\}$. If $|Z(G)| = p^2$ then $G = Z(G)$ is abelian. If $|Z(G)| = p$ then $|G/Z(G)| = p$, which is cyclic; a group with cyclic central quotient is abelian — contradiction with $|Z(G)| = p$, so $|Z(G)| = p^2$.

title: A₄ Class Equation: Concrete Verification
content: The A₄ section confirms the abstract theory concretely. A₄ (order 12, the index-2 subgroup of S₄ of even permutations) has 4 conjugacy classes of sizes 1+3+4+4 = 12: the identity, the three double-transpositions forming a Klein four-subgroup, and two classes of 3-cycles (the 3-cycles split into two A₄-classes because conjugation by an odd permutation is unavailable in A₄). `card_center_A4` confirms Z(A₄) = {e} (trivial center) — consistent with A₄ not being a p-group (12 = 2²·3, not a prime power). `A4_not_comm` uses `decide` (kernel-level) while the larger conjugacy enumerations use `native_decide` (compiled bytecode), a deliberate trust-vs-speed tradeoff.
mathContext: $|A_4| = 12$, conjugacy class sizes: $1, 3, 4, 4$ (total 12 ✓). $Z(A_4) = \{e\}$, $|Z(A_4)| = 1$. Class structure: $\{e\}$, $V_4 \setminus \{e\}$ (double-transpositions, conjugate in $A_4$ because $V_4$ is normal), and two 3-cycle classes that fuse into a single $S_4$-class but split in $A_4$. The 3-cycle splitting in $A_4$ is the simplest example of class fusion under restriction to an index-2 normal subgroup — controlled by whether the centralizer in $S_4$ is contained in $A_4$ (here it is, so the class splits).
relatedConcepts: class splitting under index-2 normal subgroups

title: The Class Equation as the Bridge to Character Theory
content: The class equation has a much deeper structural meaning than the cardinality identity proved here: it is the **conjugacy-class side of Brauer's permutation lemma**, which states that for a finite group $G$ over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, the number of irreducible representations equals the number of conjugacy classes. The class function $\chi: G \to \mathbb{C}$ assigning to each $g$ the trace of its representation matrix is constant on conjugacy classes (by trace-invariance under conjugation), so the space of class functions has dimension equal to $|\text{ConjClasses}(G)|$. Character orthogonality then identifies this dimension with the number of irreducible characters. The orbit-centralizer identity $|[x]| = [G:C_G(x)]$ also reappears in this setting as the formula $|G| = \sum_\chi (\chi(1))^2$ (sum of squared dimensions of irreducible representations equals group order) when paired with the second orthogonality relation. The fact that this file proves the class equation cleanly via `index_comap_of_surjective` provides the cardinality foundation that any future Mathlib formalization of character theory will build on.
mathContext: **Class functions**: $\{f: G \to \mathbb{C} \mid f(gxg^{-1}) = f(x)\}$ form a $\mathbb{C}$-vector space of dimension $|\text{ConjClasses}(G)|$. **Brauer's permutation lemma**: $|\text{Irr}(G)| = |\text{ConjClasses}(G)|$. **Class equation in rep-theory form**: $|G| = \sum_{\chi \in \text{Irr}(G)} \chi(1)^2 = \sum_{[x]} [G : C_G(x)] \cdot |[x]|^{-1} \cdot |[x]| = \sum_{[x]} [G : C_G(x)]$ when grouped by representative — the two sides agree term-by-term. **For p-groups**: every irreducible representation has dimension a power of $p$ (because $\chi(1) \mid |G|$ for any $\chi$). Combined with $\sum \chi(1)^2 = p^k$, this gives strong constraints on the representation theory of p-groups that mirror the class-equation argument for center nontriviality.
relatedConcepts: sum of squares formula |G| = Σ χ(1)²
